title: Pipeline economics
description: Per component: what it consumes (CPU, memory), what it moves (msg/s per hop and the deltas between hops), how long it takes (latency per hop) and what it costs (millicores of CPU per msg/s of pipeline throughput). The headline row divides each stage's CPU by the TBMQ incoming publish rate, so a stage that is expensive per message stands out regardless of load. TLS CAVEAT: nothing in this cluster attributes CPU to TLS -- neither the kernel, the JVM nor cAdvisor separates encryption from the rest of a process. The TLS row therefore shows only proxies (how many sessions are TLS, handshake/accept rate, bytes moved over those sockets); no panel here claims to measure the CPU cost of TLS, and none should be read that way.

panels.title: Pipeline message rate
panels.description: TBMQ incoming publishes: the denominator of every cost-per-message panel on this board.

panels.title: Chain CPU
panels.description: Cores burned by everything in thingsboard-mqtt-broker + iot-pipeline + iot-storage.

panels.title: Chain cost per message
panels.description: Millicores per msg/s across the whole chain. This includes the fixed overhead that does not scale with load, so it falls as throughput rises.

panels.title: Observability cost per message
panels.description: What it costs to watch the pipeline: the whole monitoring namespace per pipeline msg/s.

panels.title: Cost of a TBMQ broker RPC
panels.description: Internal Kafka CPU divided by its Produce+Fetch+OffsetCommit rate.

panels.title: Cost of an app Kafka RPC
Cost per message by stage
panels.description: Millicores of CPU per msg/s of pipeline throughput, per stage. The longest bar is where the pipeline burns its budget. Stages 11-13 are overhead, not message path.

panels.title: Cost per message by stage over time
panels.description: Stacked: the top of the stack is the chain cost per message. A stage whose band widens while the others hold is getting less efficient, not just busier.

panels.title: CPU cores by stage
panels.description: container_cpu_usage_seconds_total, pause containers excluded.

panels.title: Memory vs its limit, per pod
panels.description: A pod sitting near 1.0 is one OOMKill away from a restart.

panels.title: CPU throttling
panels.description: Only pods with a CPU limit can be throttled, and on this cluster that is KEDA and the Strimzi operator alone -- every pipeline pod runs without a CPU limit, so an empty chart here means 'no limits configured', not 'no CPU pressure'. Node-level headroom is in the Saturation row.

panels.title: Messages per second at each hop
panels.description: Hops 01-11 should sit on top of each other at the sensor rate. Hops 12-13 are one vehicle per ~3 detections, and 14-15 are larger because ClickHouse also reads vehicles/traffic/sensor-health and fans every row out into materialised views.

panels.title: Delta between consecutive hops (msg/s lost or buffered)
panels.description: Positive = the downstream stage is behind or dropping; negative = it is catching up on a backlog. Sustained non-zero on one line localises the loss to that hop.

panels.title: Rejected, dropped, lost and duplicate counters
panels.description: Every counter in the chain that means 'this message did not make it'. Flat at zero is the expected picture.

panels.title: Rejections by reason (telemetry-processor) and rejected rows
panels.description: telemetry-processor is the only stage that classifies why it drops a record; the rows it writes out land in iot.detections_rejected (see the Tunnel traffic board).

panels.title: End-to-end latency percentiles (ClickHouse, iot.detections)
panels.description: The only true per-message end-to-end timings in the system: they come from timestamps carried on the message itself (ts, received_ts, processed_ts, inserted_at).

targets.rawSql:
SELECT $__timeInterval(ts) AS time,
  quantile(0.50)(mqtt_latency_ms) / 1000 AS sensor_to_tbmq_p50,
  quantile(0.95)(mqtt_latency_ms) / 1000 AS sensor_to_tbmq_p95,
  quantile(0.50)(process_latency_ms) / 1000 AS tbmq_to_processor_p50,
  quantile(0.95)(process_latency_ms) / 1000 AS tbmq_to_processor_p95,
  quantile(0.50)(ingest_latency_ms) / 1000 AS tbmq_to_clickhouse_p50,
  quantile(0.95)(ingest_latency_ms) / 1000 AS tbmq_to_clickhouse_p95
FROM iot.detections
WHERE $__timeFilter(ts)
GROUP BY time
ORDER BY time

panels.title: Inside TBMQ: where the broker's time goes (avg)
panels.description: Micrometer timers on TBMQ's actuator endpoint. 'commitSync' is per pack, and TBMQ commits once per pack -- see the Kafka efficiency row for what that costs.

panels.title: Python stages: histogram percentiles
panels.description: The only histograms the Python services export (telemetry_processor: batch_duration, batch_ack, event_age; consensus: event_age). Neither service times an individual record end to end, so there is no per-record p99 to show.

panels.title: Queued work: lag, backlog and in-flight records
panels.description: Kafka Exporter lag per group, plus each service's own view of its backlog. The consensus consumer group is deliberately excluded from the exporter series: consensus manages its own offsets for replay, so the exporter's number for it is meaningless -- consensus_kafka_lag_records is the real unread count.

panels.title: TBMQ internal Kafka: RPCs per record
panels.description: Client-facing broker calls divided by records written to the broker.

panels.title: App Kafka: RPCs per record
panels.description: Same formula as the panel to its left. The gap between the two numbers is the whole story.

panels.title: TBMQ: messages per commitSync
panels.description: TBMQ commits its consumer offsets once per pack, so this is also the average pack size. Small packs mean one OffsetCommit RPC and one __consumer_offsets write per handful of messages.

panels.title: Broker RPCs per record, both clusters
panels.description: tbmq-kafka pays several times what app-kafka pays for the same record, because TBMQ commitSync()s after every small pack while the pipeline producers batch.

panels.title: Request rate by type and cluster
panels.description: The absolute RPC volume behind the ratio above.

panels.title: __consumer_offsets write rate
panels.description: Offset commits are real writes to a real log. On tbmq-kafka this topic carries a sizeable fraction of a record per message that ever reaches a sensor payload.

panels.title: Average records per Produce request
panels.description: How well each cluster's producers batch. Payload topics only (__consumer_offsets is written by the coordinator, not by a Produce request).

panels.title: Partitions, leaders and topics per cluster
panels.description: Every partition costs a fetch session, a log directory and a share of the broker's background work whether or not it carries traffic.

panels.title: Messages in per topic
panels.description: Includes __consumer_offsets, which is exactly the point.

panels.title: TLS (proxies only -- no metric attributes CPU to TLS)
TLS sessions
panels.description: TBMQ counts SSL sessions separately; equal to the total means every MQTT client is on TLS.

panels.title: MQTT bytes/s over TLS sockets
panels.description: PROXY: all traffic on the broker pods' interfaces, which is MQTT-over-TLS plus plaintext Kafka, Redis, Postgres and scrape traffic. It is an upper bound on bytes encrypted, not a measurement of them.

panels.title: TLS handshakes/s (proxy: connections accepted)
panels.description: PROXY: every accepted MQTT connection implies one TLS handshake, the most expensive single TLS operation. At steady state with long-lived sessions this is ~0, which is why handshake cost does not show up in the steady-state cost-per-message numbers.

panels.title: Connection churn/s
panels.description: Disconnects plus errors: churn here turns into handshake load on the panel to the left.

panels.title: Connection and handshake events/s
panels.description: PROXY for TLS work. A reconnect storm is the one time TLS cost is visible, as a correlated spike here and in the broker's CPU line.

panels.title: Network bytes per pod on the message path
panels.description: Only the MQTT listener is TLS-terminated; the Kafka, Valkey and Postgres hops on this cluster are in-cluster plaintext. Comparing the broker's line with the rest shows how much of the total byte volume even passes through TLS.

panels.title: Node CPU used
panels.description: Cores busy across the whole node, pipeline and everything else.

panels.title: CPU requested / allocatable
panels.description: What the scheduler thinks is booked. Far below actual usage means requests are set too low for the scheduler to protect anything.

panels.title: Node CPU and memory over time
panels.description: If 'cores busy' approaches 'cores on the node' the node is the limit; until then the pipeline is limited by its own concurrency, not by hardware.

panels.title: Replicas vs their KEDA maximum
panels.description: A stage pinned at its maximum while its lag grows is the stage that needs more room.

panels.title: KEDA scaler value vs threshold
panels.description: The lag value KEDA is actually scaling on.

panels.title: Pod restarts (1h increase) on the message path
